title: "Trusted by" is not "Fidato da"
rule: Social-proof lines translate the intent, not the words. "Fidato da" is a literal calque of "Trusted by" and reads as machine output. Use "Scelto da", "Usato da" or "Già X aziende lo usano".

title: "Powered by" and English taglines
rule: Taglines such as "Powered by AI" or "Multi-platform" must be translated like any other copy: "Basato sull'IA", "Con tecnologia IA", "Multipiattaforma".

title: Quantities: "oltre", not "+"
rule: Italian copy expresses "15.000+" as "oltre 15.000" and never glues the sign to the noun ("6+piattaforme"). The plus sign is an English convention.

title: Thousands with a dot, words for big numbers
rule: Italian groups thousands with a dot and uses a decimal comma: 9.500, 2,5. "9,500" means nine and a half. In headlines write "miliardi" instead of abbreviations such as "Mld".

title: No leftover English on an Italian page
rule: Buttons, badges, section headers, list endings and feature bullets must all be Italian. Leftover English ("SALE", "Explore all features") and CMS placeholders ("Secondary text") are release bugs. Product and brand names stay as they are.

title: Sentence case, not Title Case; ALL CAPS is fine
rule: Italian headings, buttons and calls to action capitalise only the first word and proper nouns. English Title Case ("Pronto per Iniziare?") looks translated. The rule is about mixed capitals only: a heading set in ALL CAPS is a design choice and is fine, and a brand name keeps its own capitals.

title: Gender and number agreement
rule: Adjectives, articles and nouns agree in gender and number: "documenti falsi", "pagine aggiornate", "due nuovi strumenti". Machine-translated copy often agrees the adjective with the wrong noun.

title: Verbs agree with their subject
rule: A plural subject takes a plural verb: "le imprese scelgono", not "le imprese scegli". Check every verb in headings that were translated from English questions.

title: Wrong word sense
rule: Dictionary translations pick the wrong sense of a word. "Speakers" meaning people are "madrelingua" or "parlanti", never "altoparlanti" (loudspeakers). Check every word with a misleading Italian twin: "eventually" is "alla fine", not "eventualmente" (which means "possibly"); "actually" is "in realtà", not "attualmente" (currently).

title: Translate idioms by meaning
rule: English idioms need an Italian equivalent, not a word-for-word copy: "Top Picks" is "I più scelti" (not "I migliori gusti", the best flavours); "bloated" software is "sovraccarico", not "gonfio"; "game changer" is "una svolta", not "cambiatore di gioco".

title: Italian spelling of borrowed terms
rule: Derived product terms follow Italian spelling, not an invented or English-shaped form: "parafrasatore" (not "parafrasiatore"), "traduttore", "correttore". When unsure, check the term in a dictionary before shipping.

title: Characters must render
rule: Apostrophes and accented letters must survive the pipeline. "uní" in place of "un'" or "Ã¨" in place of "è" is a broken encoding, and it usually sits on the main call to action.

title: Rewrite machine word order
rule: English noun stacks ("Real Estate Photo Enhancement") cannot be mapped word by word. Rebuild the phrase with Italian order and a verb where a heading needs one: "Migliora le foto degli immobili".
prefer: Migliora le foto degli immobili con l'IA

title: One name per feature
rule: A feature keeps one Italian name across the page and the product. Two spellings or two translations of the same tool ("parafrasatore" and "Parafrasiatore") read as carelessness.

title: "IA" or "AI": either, never mixed
rule: Both "IA" (intelligenza artificiale) and the English "AI" are correct in Italian product copy; our field practice prefers "IA" in running text. A single string that uses either form is fine. Flag only a text that mixes the two.
